questions.title: What is the expected sensory and motor finding below a complete spinal cord transection?
questions.question: A patient sustains a traumatic injury with complete transection of the spinal cord at the T8 level. Which of the following is expected below the level of the lesion?

options.A: Total loss of all sensory modalities with bilateral paraplegia
options.B: Ipsilateral loss of proprioception only, with normal power
options.C: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature only
options.D: Preserved sensation with isolated bilateral leg weakness

explanations.A: Correct. Complete transection severs every ascending and descending pathway bilaterally at that level, so below the lesion there is total loss of all sensory modalities (touch, pain, temperature, proprioception, vibration) together with bilateral paraplegia from loss of all descending motor control. This is unlike partial cord syndromes, which selectively spare specific tracts because only part of the cord's cross-section is damaged. Recognising this all-or-nothing pattern is the first step in distinguishing complete transection from Brown-Séquard or anterior cord syndrome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Isolated ipsilateral proprioceptive loss with normal power describes a partial dorsal-column lesion, not complete transection, which abolishes power and every sensory modality bilaterally.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Isolated contralateral pain/temperature loss describes anterior cord syndrome (dorsal columns spared), not complete transection, which spares nothing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complete transection abolishes sensation entirely below the lesion; it does not preserve sensation while producing isolated motor weakness.

questions.learning_objective: State that complete spinal cord transection causes bilateral paraplegia with total sensory loss below the lesion, unlike partial cord syndromes.

questions.title: The fourth ventricle develops as the cavity of which embryonic brain vesicle?
questions.question: The fourth ventricle is the cerebrospinal fluid-filled cavity of which primary embryonic brain vesicle?

explanations.A: Correct. The fourth ventricle is the cavity of the rhombencephalon (hindbrain). The third ventricle is the cavity of the diencephalon, and the cerebral aqueduct is the cavity of the mesencephalon. Each major ventricular cavity maps to a specific embryonic brain vesicle in this way.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The prosencephalon (forebrain) gives rise to the telencephalon and diencephalon, whose cavities are the lateral ventricles and third ventricle, not the fourth ventricle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The mesencephalon (midbrain) gives rise to the narrow cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius, not the fourth ventricle.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The telencephalon's cavities are the paired lateral ventricles, not the fourth ventricle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the fourth ventricle develops as the cavity of the rhombencephalon (hindbrain).

questions.title: Which fissure divides the cerebellum into anterior and posterior lobes?
questions.question: Which fissure of the cerebellum separates the anterior lobe from the posterior lobe?

explanations.A: Correct. The primary fissure is the deepest and most prominent fissure on the superior surface of the cerebellum. It divides the cerebellum into the anterior lobe and the posterior lobe. The anterior/posterior lobe distinction it defines underlies the spinocerebellum's functional territory.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterolateral fissure separates the posterior lobe from the flocculonodular lobe, not the anterior lobe from the posterior lobe.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The horizontal fissure runs along the lateral cerebellar surface and is not the landmark dividing anterior from posterior lobe.
explanations.D: Incorrect. There is no uvulonodular fissure marking the anterior/posterior lobe boundary; the uvula and nodule are components of the vermis and flocculonodular lobe respectively.

questions.learning_objective: Name the primary fissure as the landmark dividing the cerebellum into anterior and posterior lobes.

questions.title: Into which pathway does the spinal lemniscus continue?
questions.question: The lateral spinothalamic pathway, ascending through the spinal cord as the 'spinal lemniscus', continues rostrally into the brainstem as which tract?

explanations.A: Correct. The spinal lemniscus, formed by second-order lateral spinothalamic fibres, continues rostrally as the neospinothalamic tract. This is a fast, few-synapse pathway carrying sharp, well-localised pain directly to the ventral posterolateral thalamic nucleus. It contrasts with the slower, multisynaptic paleospinothalamic pathway, which carries dull, poorly localised pain via the reticular formation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medial lemniscus carries dorsal column-mediated fine touch/proprioception, formed by internal arcuate fibres from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, a separate pathway from the spinal lemniscus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The trigeminothalamic tract carries facial (not body) pain/temperature and touch sensation via the trigeminal system, a separate pathway from the spinal lemniscus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal column pathway is a distinct, uncrossed system for fine touch/proprioception, unrelated to the spinothalamic spinal lemniscus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the neospinothalamic tract as the rostral continuation of the spinal lemniscus (lateral spinothalamic pathway).

questions.title: Into which vein does the common facial vein drain?
questions.question: The common facial vein, formed by union of the facial and retromandibular veins, drains directly into which vessel?

explanations.A: Correct. The common facial vein is formed in the upper neck by union of the facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein. It then crosses superficial to the carotid sheath and drains directly into the internal jugular vein. This gives the internal jugular vein several individually named tributaries along its course.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The external jugular vein is formed chiefly by the posterior division of the retromandibular vein together with the posterior auricular vein, a separate drainage route from the common facial vein.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The subclavian vein receives the external jugular vein at the neck's root, not the common facial vein directly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The cavernous sinus receives blood via the superior ophthalmic vein and emissary veins, not directly from the common facial vein, though facial vein infection can spread intracranially by this valveless route.
